story.title: The Eleventh Refill
story.logline: A night-shift pharmacist in Karachi finds a dead man's heart pills are still being collected every month, and the trail leads to the one doctor she owes everything.
story.text:
Asma Qureshi kept the night ledger in pencil because Mr. Rizvi, who owned the shop and trusted nothing else, trusted pencil. Ink was for people who never made mistakes, he said. He had said it the day he hired her and at least twice a month since, usually while correcting her arithmetic.

At twenty to three on a Thursday the generator in the alley coughed, the tube light over the antibiotics went the color of weak tea, and a boy in a cricket jersey two sizes too big slid a prescription under the glass.

Amlodipine, ten milligrams. Thirty tablets. Anwar Siddiqui.

She had filled it before. She flipped the ledger back one page, then four, then all the way to March, and the pencil stub in her hand started to feel like evidence. Eleven times. Same tablets, same signature at the bottom: Dr. Fareeha Naqvi, the one doctor in Saddar who had once found Asma's mother a bed at Civil when the ward boys were saying there were none.

Anwar Siddiqui had been buried in March. Asma knew because his widow had come in the week after, still in white, holding an unopened box of insulin, and asked very politely whether the pharmacy gave refunds.

"Who's it for?" Asma asked.

"My nana."

"And your nana's name?"

The boy looked at the street, where a motorbike idled with its headlight off. He took the prescription back, folded it once, and walked out the way boys walk when someone has told them not to run.

On the counter he'd left exact change, the notes folded in thirds. Same as every month. On the back of the fifty, in blue ballpoint, someone had written a phone number.

* * *

She did not call it that night. She did the stock count instead, and the stock count was wrong in a way it had been wrong for a year: amlodipine short by thirty, every month, balanced by a line in her own handwriting she didn't remember writing.

storyBible.synopsis: Asma Qureshi, a meticulous night-shift pharmacist in Saddar, notices that a dead man's heart medication has been collected every month since his funeral. The boy who brings the prescription leaves exact change and a phone number. The number belongs to Dr. Fareeha Naqvi, the doctor who once saved Asma's mother, and who has been writing prescriptions in dead patients' names to keep poor ones alive. The missing stock is covered by ledger lines in Asma's own handwriting. As Mr. Rizvi starts counting too, Asma has to decide whether to expose the person she owes everything to, or admit she chose a side months ago.
themes: who counts, and who gets counted
storyBible.world: Saddar, Karachi, now. A 24-hour medical store on a street of shuttered wholesalers, running on a generator through the load-shedding. Prescriptions are paper, ledgers are pencil, and everyone knows which doctor will see you for free if you come after Isha.

characters.name: Asma Qureshi
characters.want: To keep her job and her record clean
characters.need: To admit she has already chosen a side
characters.wound: Her mother nearly died waiting for a hospital bed
characters.secret: Some of the ledger lines covering the missing stock are in her handwriting
characters.contradiction: Exact with numbers, evasive about herself
characters.voice: Dry, precise, clipped. Switches to Urdu when cornered. Answers questions with questions.

characters.name: Bilal
characters.role: Errand runner who brings the prescription
characters.need: An adult who tells him the truth about what he carries
characters.wound: A father who left for Dubai and stopped calling
characters.secret: He knows exactly who the medicine is for
characters.contradiction: Street-tough, but folds every note neatly because his mother taught him to
characters.voice: Short answers, cricket slang, never says a name.

characters.name: Dr. Fareeha Naqvi
characters.want: To keep her poorest patients alive
characters.need: To stop making other people carry her risk
characters.wound: Thirty years of watching the public hospital turn people away
characters.secret: She writes prescriptions for the dead and sends the pills to the living
characters.contradiction: A healer who has grown comfortable lying
characters.arc: From hidden saint to exposed sinner, and maybe both
characters.voice: Warm, unhurried, formal English with Urdu courtesies; calls everyone "beta"; never raises her voice.

characters.name: Iqbal Rizvi
characters.need: To see what his rules cost people
characters.wound: Lost his first shop to a partner who cooked the books
characters.secret: He noticed the shortage months ago and said nothing
characters.arc: From suspicious boss to quiet accomplice
characters.voice: Proverbs, arithmetic and complaints about the electricity. Repeats himself for emphasis.

u1.script:
# Episode 1: Exact Change

EXT. SADDAR - RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - NIGHT

A shuttered street. One shop still lit: RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - 24 HOURS. A generator thuds in the alley.

INT. RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - NIGHT

ASMA QURESHI (29), dupatta pinned back with a black bulldog clip, writes in a ledger with a pencil stub worn to her fingertips.

The tube light browns out. Comes back.

A hand slides a prescription under the glass. The BOY (12), in a faded cricket jersey that reaches his knees.

ASMA
(not looking up)
Name?

BOY
It's written.

She reads. Stops. Flips the ledger back a page. Four pages. All the way to March.

INSERT - LEDGER
The same line, again and again: "Anwar Siddiqui - Amlodipine 10mg."

ASMA
Who is it for?

BOY
My nana.

ASMA
What's your nana's name?

His eyes go to the street. A motorbike idles there, headlight off.

He takes the prescription back. Folds it once. Walks out, carefully not running.

ASMA
Your pills --

On the counter: exact change, folded in thirds.

She unfolds the fifty. On the back, in blue ballpoint, a phone number.

SMASH TO BLACK.

u2.script:
# Episode 2: Pencil

INT. ASMA'S HOME - BEDROOM - DAWN

A narrow room shared with a sewing machine. ASMA lies on top of the bedsheet in yesterday's kameez, the fifty-rupee note on her chest. The ceiling fan ticks. Her MOTHER coughs through the wall.

She turns the note over. The phone number. She reaches for her phone. Stops.

INT. RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - STOCKROOM - NIGHT

Cartons to the ceiling. Asma counts amlodipine boxes with a pencil behind her ear.

ASMA
(under her breath)
Twenty-eight. Twenty-nine.

She checks the ledger. Thirty short. Then, under the shortfall, a correction in pencil. She knows the loops of those letters.

ASMA
That's my hand.

She erases it. Underneath, another line. Older.

INT. RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - DAWN

Grey light through the shutter. MR. RIZVI (63), in a pressed shalwar kameez and a cardigan in May, lets himself in two hours early, too cheerful.

MR. RIZVI
The electricity came back at four. Four! I thought, God has forgiven Karachi, let me go and count something.

ASMA
Everything's counted.

MR. RIZVI
Everything is always counted, beta. Counting is not the problem. The problem is adding.

He picks up the fifty-rupee note from the counter. Turns it over.

INT. ASMA'S HOME - BEDROOM - DAY

Asma sits on the bed and dials. It rings once.

u3.script:
# Episode 3: The Doctor Is In

INT. ASMA'S HOME - BEDROOM - DAY

The phone at her ear. Laundry shadows move across the wall.

DR. NAQVI (V.O.)
Asma. I wondered when.

ASMA
You know my name.

DR. NAQVI (V.O.)
I know your mother's blood pressure. Come to the clinic after Isha. Come hungry, I have too much biryani.

INT. NAQVI CLINIC - NIGHT

A waiting room with more patients than chairs. A ceiling fan, a calendar from a drug company, a framed degree going brown at the edges.

DR. FAREEHA NAQVI (58), reading glasses on a beaded chain, waves Asma past the queue. Nobody complains, which is its own warning.

INT. NAQVI CLINIC - OFFICE - NIGHT

A desk with two chairs and a prescription pad. Dr. Naqvi pours tea.

DR. NAQVI
Anwar Siddiqui died in February. His wife did not. Her heart is not interested in paperwork.

ASMA
So you write it in his name.

DR. NAQVI
I write it in the name that gets it filled.

She tears off a fresh prescription and slides it across the desk.

DR. NAQVI
One more. For your mother, this time. Then we are the same, you and I.

Asma looks at the name on it. Her own mother's.

INT. RIZVI MEDICAL STORE - NIGHT

The tube light browns out. Asma, alone, sets the prescription on the ledger and picks up the pencil.
